newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia stocks extend losses after NATO snub.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia stocks extend losses after NATO snub.

text.p: Slovenia's floundering stock market continued to reel on news the U.S. would not back the country's bid for early NATO membership, and analysts warned on Monday the fledgling bourse had yet to see the worst.

The blue-chip SBI index has lost 6.7 percent since the U.S. said on Thursday it did not believe the small ex-Yugoslav republic was ready to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) in its first round of expansion in 1999.
Domestic market watchers warned that leaving Slovenia outside the western defence alliance's umbrella could easily shave off another 10 percent from prices over the summer.

"Remaining outside of NATO means that Slovenia will remain closed to international capital therefore, the decision will have a very negative psychological effect on the market," Mateja Gubanec, a broker at "A" banka, said.
"Domestic capital alone will not be able to improve liquidity on the market or push prices up," added Nena Jarc, a trader at Nova Ljubljanska banka.

The market has lost 27.6 percent since February, and turnover has dwindled to a tenth of their previous level. In February, the Bank of Slovenia ordered foreigners to open fiduciary accounts at any of the country's 14 fully-licensed banks to trade in Slovenian securities.
The central bank also said the money paid into accounts would have to be considered as foreign liabilities, which would have to be balanced against foreign assets.

Banks said that because of the costs involved in the balancing procedures, the accounts would cost some 12 percent of the amount handled. International investors have balked at such high fees, but there are few signs the banks are willing to back down.

"The only thing that would help the market in the short-term would be a change in the Bank of Slovenia's policy towards international portfolio investors," said Toni Apollonio, an analyst at "A" banka.
But the central bank said earlier there was no chance the fiduciary account scheme would be amended before Slovenia becomes an associated member of the European Union (EU).
"Despite that, I believe the bank might reconsider its stance because of the pressure coming from all sides as foreigners claim Slovenia is closing up to foreign capital," Apollonio said.

The market was further disappointed in June when the Constitutional Court said Slovenia needed to change the constitution to allow foreigners to buy land before parliament could ratify the association accord with the EU, which was signed a year ago.
But so far, parliamentary parties have failed to reach an agreement on when to take a vote on the constitutional changes, which require a two-thirds majority.
The European Commission said speedy ratification of the agreement was necessary for Slovenia to be included in the first round of the EU's own enlargement.
"If Slovenia is not included in the first wave of the EU enlargement, that could weigh on the country's credit ratings, and that would keep international investors away for years," an analyst said.
